goals: Explain how random forests decorrelate trees
why: Random forest is the most reliable "first serious model" for tabular data: strong accuracy with little tuning, no scaling, robust to outliers.
explain: A random forest is **bagging with decision trees + one extra twist**: at every split, each tree may only consider a **random subset of features**.

Why? If one feature is very strong, every bagged tree splits on it first and the trees look alike. Averaging similar trees helps little. Random feature subsets make the trees **diverse**, and diverse errors cancel better.
A committee of varied experts beats a committee of clones. That is the whole idea.

Key hyperparameters: **n_estimators** (more is better, up to cost), **max_features** (√p for classification is the classic default), and **min_samples_leaf** / **max_depth** for smoothing. Use **permutation importance** or SHAP rather than default impurity importance.

example.title: How often is the star feature off the menu?
steps: A churn dataset has p = 16 features; the classification default offers m = √16 = 4 at each split
Features not offered at a split: 16 − 4 = 12
Chance "days since last login" is excluded: 12 / 16 = 0.75, so about 75% of splits (including most trees' first split) must use another feature
With p = 100 and m = 10 the exclusion chance is 90 / 100 = 0.90
example.result: Even a dominant feature is unavailable most of the time, which forces trees to find other patterns and makes them less alike. Diverse trees average out better.

mistakes: Expecting it to extrapolate beyond the training range (trees predict flat beyond the data).
Huge forests on huge data without considering memory.
avoid: When the smallest, fastest or most interpretable model is required
interview: How does a random forest differ from bagging?
Why does it rarely overfit as trees are added?

practice.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True, as_frame=True)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=0)
rf = RandomForestClassifier(500, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(round(rf.score(X_te, y_te), 3))
imp = permutation_importance(rf, X_te, y_te, n_repeats=5, random_state=0)
print(sorted(zip(imp.importances_mean.round(3), X.columns), reverse=True)[:5])

check.q: What does a random forest add on top of bagging?
options: A random feature subset at each split

check.q: Does a random forest need feature scaling?
check.why: Tree splits are unaffected by scale.

formula.plain: Out of p features, m are offered at each split; any given feature is left off the menu in (p − m) / p of the splits.
